title: The Strange History of the Game Boy Camera
creator: Pixel Archive
description:
In 1998 Nintendo released a camera for the Game Boy. It shot 128 by 112 pixels in four shades of grey, and for a while it was the world's smallest digital camera. Here's how it happened and why people still use it today.

Archive footage courtesy of the community scans in the comments.

Support the channel: https://ko-fi.com/pixelarchive

sentences.t: In 1998, Nintendo released a camera that plugged into the top of a Game Boy.
It took photos at a hundred and twenty-eight by a hundred and twelve pixels, in four shades of grey.
And for a while, it was listed as the smallest digital camera in the world.
Today we're looking at how that happened, and why people are still shooting with it almost thirty years later.
So, the late nineties.
Digital cameras existed, but they were expensive, often hundreds of dollars, and most people had never touched one.
At the same time, the Game Boy was almost ten years old and still selling in huge numbers.
Nintendo had this enormous base of players who already owned the hardware, and they wanted accessories that would keep it alive.
The camera was developed together with a smaller studio, and the idea was not really photography, it was play.
You could take a picture of your face and stick it onto a little character, or use it in mini games built right into the cartridge.
Part of this video is sponsored by Lumora.
Okay, so how did it actually work?
The sensor was a tiny chip with an array of light-sensitive cells, and it fed the image straight into the Game Boy's memory.
The cartridge could hold thirty photos at a time, and then you'd have to delete some or print them.
And yes, print them, because Nintendo also sold a little thermal printer that spat out stickers on receipt paper.
Those stickers faded over the years, so a lot of the original prints from the nineties are almost blank now.
The camera head could rotate, so you could point it forward or at yourself, which, in 1998, was basically a selfie camera.
It was not a huge commercial success, but it wasn't a failure either, it sold well enough in Japan especially.
And then, like a lot of accessories, it ended up in drawers and garage sales.
But here's the interesting part.
Around the 2010s, people started digging these out again, and they discovered that the images have a really distinctive look.
Because of the four shades and the way the sensor dithers, every photo looks like a little piece of pixel art.
Photographers started modding them, adding proper lenses, so you'd see these Game Boy cameras with zoom lenses strapped to the front.
There are people who've shot entire music videos on it, frame by frame.
And there are now adapters that let you pull the photos off the cartridge onto a computer without the printer at all.
I picked one up a few months ago for about fifteen dollars, and I've been carrying it around everywhere.
These are some of the shots I took, my street, my dog, a very confused pigeon.
There's something about the limitation that makes you look harder at what's in front of you.
You only get thirty shots, the screen is tiny and green, and you have no idea if the photo is any good until you see it big.
Which is honestly kind of how film used to feel.
So, a toy camera that was never meant for real photography ended up with a whole community of artists around it.
If you've got one in a drawer somewhere, dig it out, I promise it's more fun than it has any right to be.
Thanks for watching, and I'll see you in the next one.
